title: When checking an API response, check the `status_code` and `text` first.
body: When calling an API using `requests`, check whether the call was successful using `response.status_code`, and if there is a problem, check the actual response content using `response.text`.
detail: 200-series codes usually indicate success, 404 means the resource doesn’t exist, and 500-series codes indicate a server-side issue. If you simply call `response.json()` right away, you might miss the cause of the failure, so as a beginner, it’s a good habit to check the `status_code` and `text` first. Since the response may not be in JSON format, reviewing the status code along with a portion of the body will help you identify the cause more quickly.

title: Timeouts and RequestExceptions are safeguards designed to minimize downtime.
body: `requests.get(..., timeout=10)` prevents the program from waiting indefinitely for a response. Network issues can be handled by grouping them under the `RequestException` class.
detail: If the API server is slow or the network is unstable, the program may appear to be frozen for a long time. Setting a timeout limits the waiting time, and catching a `RequestException` allows you to isolate and handle issues at the request stage, such as connection failures or timeouts. Beginners should get into the habit of including a timeout by default, as requests without one carry the risk of waiting indefinitely.

title: `raise_for_status()` raises an exception for an invalid HTTP status.
body: response.raise_for_status() raises an HTTPError when a failure status code—such as 404 or 500—is received, ensuring that the issue is not hidden. This allows you to quickly detect failed API calls.
detail: An API call is not always successful just because a response object has been returned. A 404 page or a 500 error response can also be returned as a response object. Using `raise_for_status()` prevents the code from proceeding as if it were successful and allows you to handle the failure state as an exception. This makes debugging easier, as you can then use the `except` block to handle request failures and data parsing failures separately.

title: `params` safely appends the URL query, and `response.json()` converts the JSON response into a dictionary or list.
body: In a GET request, `params` is used to pass URL query values, such as search terms. `response.json()` converts the JSON response returned by the server into a Python data structure.
detail: While you can manually append values like `?q=python` to the URL string, using the `params` dictionary can help reduce encoding and concatenation errors. However, since `response.json()` is only safe when the response is actually JSON, it’s best to use it in conjunction with a flow that checks the `status_code` and `text`.
